column1: What did the PMCSA provide?
column2: Independent advice to the Prime Minister on science in its very broadest sense.

column1: Are there other Chief Science Advisors besides the PM's?
column2: Yes - across Health, Environment, Justice, Treasury, Transport, Education, Conservation and many other agencies.

column1: Is science the only advice a government receives?
column2: No. Science is never the only advice.

column1: What are science's two named strengths in a policy setting?
column2: Defining the problem, and identifying options.

column1: What does science struggle with in a policy setting?
column2: Definitive timely answers.

column1: Why does science's weakness matter politically?
column2: Politicians have to make decisions within defined timeframes.

column1: Who bridges the gap between science and political decision-making?
column2: Policy makers.

column1: What is said about presenting the facts?
column2: Presenting the "facts" rarely changed anyone's mind.

column1: State the warning about proxy debates.
column2: Science debate should not be a proxy for values debate.

column1: Name the three types of science advice.
column2: Proactive with recommendations, proactive public-facing explainers without recommendations, and reactive.

column1: Give two examples of proactive advice with recommendations.
column2: Plastics and AI in healthcare (also commercial fisheries, antimicrobial resistance, food waste).

column1: Give two examples of public-facing explainers without recommendations.
column2: 5G and cannabis (also fluoride and nitrate).

column1: Give two examples of reactive advice.
column2: The mosque shooting and Whakaari White Island (also COVID-19).

column1: Why do explainers deliberately omit recommendations?
column2: They cover contested-values topics, where recommending invites the science to be attacked as a proxy for the values fight.

column1: Why is plastic a wicked rather than merely complex problem?
column2: Microplastics are already everywhere in everything, so it is probably not solvable - only ameliorable.

column1: What property made plastic attractive, and why was that ironic?
column2: It was hard to destroy and very stable - which is exactly why it will not go away.

column1: Roughly how much plastic had been made at the time of the report?
column2: About 8.3 billion tonnes.

column1: What was the plastics report's tagline?
column2: Make best practice, standard practice.

column1: What did the tagline imply about the recommendations?
column2: They were largely not new technical insights, but good existing practice that could be adopted more widely and scaled.

column1: Name three of the six plastics report themes.
column2: A national plastic action plan; embed rethinking plastic in government; consistent design, use and disposal (also innovate and amplify, tackle environmental and health impacts, collect data).

column1: Name four conditions that helped the plastics report land.
column2: A committed minister, public pressure including letters from children, polling showing plastic as the top environmental concern, and easy expert panel recruitment.

column1: What caveat did the lecturer give about plastic being the top public concern?
column2: It was probably not the most important issue - tractability and importance are different things.

column1: What happened after the plastics report launched?
column2: Policy officials' work, advice to accept, Cabinet approval, and a commitment in the 2020 Speech from the Throne.

column1: Name three single-use items phased out in the August 2020 announcement.
column2: Plastic straws, drink stirrers, and produce bags (also tableware and non-compostable fruit stickers).

column1: What happens to the technical adviser once recommendations are accepted?
column2: They step away; it is up to politicians and policy people to implement.

column1: Why did the polystyrene clamshell phase-out take time?
column2: Replacement products had to be found that worked and that suppliers accepted, and existing stock had to be used up.

column1: Did the plastics work survive a change of government?
column2: Yes - by 2024 the waste transformation plan was still in play and the plastics 1, 2 and 5 recommendation went through under the new coalition.

column1: Which recommendation appeared in every report over six years?
column2: Collecting data.

column1: Why is data collection hard to fund?
column2: Governments want to announce shiny new policies that make a difference now; data is resource-intensive and hard to get public support for.

column1: Why is data collection nonetheless argued to be the best investment?
column2: It is what lets you test whether all the other policies actually worked.

column1: In the plastics data picture, what was essentially unknown?
column2: How much plastic is lost to the environment.

column1: What instruction follows from the absence of clean data?
column2: Understand your level of confidence, and map that uncertainty through to your options and recommendations.

column1: Name the three crises handled reactively during the PMCSA tenure.
column2: The Christchurch mosque shooting, the Whakaari White Island eruption, and COVID-19.

column1: What did the mosque shooting advice inform?
column2: What became the Christchurch Call.

column1: What was the operative question after the Whakaari eruption?
column2: What is the probability of a second eruption?

column1: Name three elements of the volcanic risk communication machinery.
column2: The NZ Volcano Science Advisory Panel, consistent messaging, and media engagement.

column1: Why does consistent messaging matter in a crisis?
column2: So experts do not contradict each other in public while people are making safety decisions.

column1: What does Volpara Health do?
column2: Image analysis of mammograms, providing a breast density score - an independent breast cancer risk factor.

column1: How widely is Volpara used?
column2: In over 40% of US breast cancer screenings.

column1: What does Formus do?
column2: Builds a 3D model of the hip joint so surgeons can plan interventions virtually - "plan from a scan" in under an hour.

column1: What problem does Formus solve for surgeons?
column2: Previously they could not know the size and shape of the implant needed until they opened the patient up.

column1: What evaluation problem is specific to AI tools?
column2: The tool keeps changing itself, so it may make new mistakes after you have evaluated it.

column1: Why does an AI plus a person beat two people or two AIs on a radiology scan?
column2: Because humans and AI make different types of mistakes, so their errors are decorrelated.

column1: Name three considerations for AI in the national context.
column2: Evaluation tools for fitness for purpose, maintaining public social license, and supporting clinicians to trust the tools.

column1: Name four of the eight AI-in-healthcare themes.
column2: Mapping the landscape, maintaining the human element of care, enabling adoption, establishing confidence and trust (also tackling inequity, te ao Maori, data and systems, exploring future opportunities).

column1: How is "maintaining the human element of care" made concrete?
column2: If AI takes the notes, clinicians are more available for caring and eye contact.

column1: What is said about AI and data quality?
column2: AI is only as good as the data it is fed; if the data is a shambles the output will be too.

column1: Name three of the six AI guiding principles.
column2: Implementing Te Tiriti o Waitangi and recognising tikanga Maori, safe and effective AI, and AI for equity.

column1: What are the three possible fates of science advice?
column2: It may be used well, misused, or ignored.

column1: Why did the gangs report fail to land?
column2: The government and its position on crime changed between commissioning and delivery, so a harm-based report no longer suited the new policy direction.

column1: What went wrong in the gangs report media handling?
column2: A soundbite was played to the Leader of the Opposition, who dismissed it - before he had been briefed on the report.

column1: What tool came out of the gangs report failure?
column2: The consensus quadrant.

column1: Name the two axes of the consensus quadrant.
column2: Scientific consensus on the y-axis, values consensus on the x-axis.

column1: Which archetype occupies high scientific and high values consensus?
column2: The tornado.

column1: Why is advice welcome in the tornado quadrant?
column2: Everyone agrees on the facts and on what should be done, so you can be as detailed as you like.

column1: Which archetype occupies high scientific but low values consensus?
column2: Abortion.

column1: What should scientists do in the abortion quadrant?
column2: Put down their clipboards and let the values debate play out, because it is a values debate.

column1: Which archetype occupies low scientific and low values consensus?
column2: Ecstasy, or recreational drug use.

column1: Why is the ecstasy quadrant "really dangerous ground"?
column2: There is little data and massive polarisation, so scientific debate is likely to play out through a values lens.

column1: What should you do instead of recommending in the low-low quadrant?
column2: Try to move the conversation forward rather than make specific recommendations.

column1: Which archetype occupies low scientific but high values consensus?
column2: The asteroid - everyone agrees something must be done, but nobody knows what.

column1: State the rule about where recommendations work best.
column2: Where there is reasonable consensus across the scientific spectrum and no major contest of values.

column1: Which topics sat in the consensus sweet spot?
column2: Plastic, food waste, antimicrobial resistance, and emergencies.

column1: Which PMCSA topic was described as the hardest of all?
column2: Commercial fishing.

column1: Where was COVID on the quadrant in 2020?
column2: Asteroid territory - low scientific consensus, high values consensus.

column1: Where had COVID moved by 2022?
column2: High scientific consensus, low values consensus.

column1: What is counter-intuitive about COVID's trajectory?
column2: As the science consolidated, the values consensus was lost - better evidence made the advice harder to land.

column1: Where is AI plotted on the quadrant, and why?
column2: In the middle, because opinion is divergent and people have not formed camps yet.

column1: What is the "window of opportunity" for emerging technologies?
column2: The period before polarisation sets in, when you can still have a conversation with the public and hear their concerns.
